title: Singleton Pattern
summary: Exactly one instance, globally accessible — and why that guarantee is harder, and more contested, than it looks.

slides.markdown: **Singleton** guarantees exactly one instance of a class exists for the whole application, reached through one global access point — no `new` anywhere else. It sounds harmless, but "exactly one, globally accessible" is a bigger claim than it looks: it's really a global variable with extra ceremony, which is why it's the most argued-about pattern in this group. This topic covers how to build one correctly, and — just as important — when experienced engineers reach for something else instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Singleton: exactly one instance, globally accessible
slides.markdown:
**Singleton** restricts a class to exactly one instance and provides one global point to reach it — typically a static `getInstance()` method, with the constructor made private so nothing else can create a second one.

The "big claim" part is easy to gloss over: you're asserting that *no* future requirement will ever need two of this thing — two caches, two configs for two tenants, two logger targets for two test runs. That assertion often turns out wrong.

A defensible use case: a single connection pool per process, since two pools competing for the same fixed-size connection budget would waste it. A weak use case: a single `Logger`, since most logging frameworks already support multiple named loggers without forcing Singleton on you.

Takeaway: before reaching for Singleton, name the actual reason two instances would be wrong, not just unnecessary.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: Singleton access path from multiple callers
slides.markdown:
![Three caller classes each calling ConfigManager.getInstance() and converging on the same instance](assets/singleton-convergence.svg)

No matter how many callers exist, or where they sit in the codebase, `getInstance()` always resolves to the same object — the arrows converge, they never fan out to separate instances.

That convergence is both the feature and the risk: it's convenient that any code, anywhere, can reach the same instance without it being passed in — and that same convenience is what makes Singleton usage invisible in a class's constructor signature, which the pitfall slide covers.

slides.sectionTitle: Thread-safe Singleton: double-checked locking, static holder, enum singleton
slides.markdown:
Lazy Singleton needs explicit protection against two threads both passing the "is it null?" check before either finishes construction. Three established fixes:

**Double-checked locking** — check null, lock, check null again, then construct, using a `volatile` field so a partially-constructed object is never visible to another thread.

**Static holder idiom** — put the instance in a nested static class; the JVM's class-loading guarantee gives thread safety for free, with no explicit locking.

**Enum singleton** — declare a single-value `enum`; Java guarantees enum instances are created exactly once, thread-safely, by the language itself.

The underlying idea in each case is coordinating access to shared, mutable state safely across threads — a concern that shows up constantly in concurrent object-oriented design, well beyond Singleton. Most style guides now recommend the static holder or enum forms over hand-written double-checked locking, since both eliminate the chance of writing the lock wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a correct thread-safe lazy Singleton
Pitfall: Singleton as a disguised global variable
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Singleton isn't a global variable — it's a design pattern, so it's fine to use freely."

**Why it's wrong:** a Singleton reached via `ConfigManager.getInstance()` from anywhere in the codebase has exactly the properties that make global variables dangerous: any code can read or mutate its state, the dependency doesn't show up in any constructor signature, and tests can't easily swap in a fake without reaching into static state. "Design pattern" doesn't change any of that.

**Correct model:** treat a Singleton's global reachability as a real cost, not a free convenience. If a class needs shared state, prefer passing a single, explicitly-constructed instance through constructors — you get the same "one instance" property, but the dependency is visible and swappable for tests.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Singleton vs a dependency-injected, framework-scoped single instance
slides.markdown:
Both approaches guarantee "exactly one instance" — they differ in how that instance is reached and tested.

| | How the instance is reached | Testability | Dependency visibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic Singleton | Static `getInstance()` call, from anywhere | Hard — static state resists swapping fakes | Hidden — not in any constructor signature |
| DI-managed single instance | Constructor-injected by a framework (e.g. Spring singleton scope) | Easy — inject a mock in tests | Visible — appears in the constructor |

**How to decide:** if your stack already has a DI framework, let it manage single-instance scope instead of hand-rolling `getInstance()` — you keep the "one instance" guarantee while making dependencies visible and swappable. Reach for classic Singleton mainly where no DI container is available.

slides.sectionTitle: Interview framing: "why do some consider Singleton an anti-pattern?"
slides.markdown:
When an interviewer asks "why do some consider Singleton an anti-pattern," they're testing whether you can critique a pattern you just described positively — not whether you've memorized a hot take.

The honest answer has two parts. First, the hidden-dependency problem: a class calling `ConfigManager.getInstance()` internally has an invisible coupling that doesn't show up in its constructor, making the class harder to understand and test in isolation. Second, global mutable state creates hidden coupling between unrelated parts of a codebase — two features can silently interfere with each other through the same shared instance, a common item on lists of design anti-patterns.

The strong close: Singleton isn't wrong everywhere — one connection pool per process is defensible — but it's wrong as a default choice for "I need shared state," which is how it's most commonly misused.
